title: A New AI Brain That Reads 12x Faster—But Is It for Real?
summary: Imagine you're reading a book, and to understand it, you have to compare every single word with every other word. That's basically what today's smartest AI chatbots do—and it takes a ton of computer power. But a small company in Miami says it found a shortcut. Subquadratic built a new kind of AI called SubQ. Instead of comparing all words, it only compares the ones that really matter—like skipping the boring parts. This trick, called sparse attention, lets SubQ read up to 12 times more text at once than models like ChatGPT, and it uses less energy. The company also says SubQ is just as good at coding. At first, people didn't believe them. One engineer joked it might be 'AI Theranos'—a fake breakthrough. But then Subquadratic shared results from an independent testing company, Appen. The tests showed SubQ really is faster and cheaper for certain jobs. Still, nobody outside the company can play with SubQ yet, so some experts remain cautious. One researcher compared it to running a four-minute mile: not impossible, but really hard. If SubQ works as promised, it could change how all future AIs are built—making them quicker, greener, and able to analyze whole books or codebases in one go.
why_it_matters: A smarter, lighter AI could let your future homework helper or story-writing buddy run instantly on your phone without needing a constant internet connection, and it would help the planet by using less power.

background_read: AI chatbots like ChatGPT (a popular tool people use to ask questions and get answers) compare every word you type to everything they've learned, which uses huge computers and lots of electricity.
Researchers are trying to make AI that focuses only on key words—a bit like when you skim a page for the main idea—so it can run faster and greener.
Subquadratic's SubQ is a new attempt to do that, but many past AI claims have turned out to be too good to be true.
Article_Structure: WHO: Subquadratic, a small AI company in Miami.
WHAT: Built SubQ, an AI that uses sparse attention to read up to 12 times more text and still code well.
WHERE: Developed in Miami and tested independently by the company Appen.
WHY: To make AI faster, cheaper, and able to handle huge amounts of text at once while using less energy.

perspectives.description: If SubQ really works, it could slash the electricity AI needs, making powerful assistants affordable and putting them on cheap devices everywhere.
Some experts worry that SubQ might be another empty promise, like the Theranos blood-test scandal, especially since no outsider can test it yet.
Independent tests by Appen show encouraging results, but the real proof will come when many different researchers can try SubQ on their own computers.
